blocks.md:
- **Catalysts **increase the rate of reaction by providing an alternative pathway which has a lower **activation energy**
- Catalysts can be either **homogeneous **or **heterogeneous**

- Homogeneous catalysts are those that are in the same phase as the reaction mixture
- For example, in the esterification of ethanoic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) with ethanol (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) to form ethyl ethanoate (CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) under acidic conditions:

**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**COOH (aq) + CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**OH (aq) **$\overset{H^{+}(\mathrm{aq})}{\rightarrow}$** CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**COOC**<sub>**2**</sub>**H**<sub>**5**</sub>** (aq) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l)**
- The H<sup>+</sup> is a homogeneous catalyst and like the reactants and product it is in the **aqueous** phase

- Heterogeneous catalysts are those that are in a different phase to the rest of the reaction mixture
- For example, in the Born-Haber process to form ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>) from nitrogen (N<sub>2</sub>) and hydrogen (H<sub>2</sub>) an iron (Fe) catalyst is used:
**N**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) + 3H**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) **$\overset{\mathrm{Fe}(s)}{\rightarrow}$** 2NH**<sub>**3**</sub>** (g)**
- The Fe catalyst is a heterogeneous catalyst as it is in **the** solid phase, whereas the reactants and products are all in the **gas **phase

- In **heterogeneous catalysis,** the molecules react at the surface of a solid catalyst
- The mode of action of a heterogeneous catalyst consists of the following steps:
- **Adsorption **(or **chemisorption**) of the reactants on the catalyst surface

  - The reactants diffuse to the surface of the catalyst
  - The reactant is **physically** **adsorbed** onto the surface by **weak** **forces**
  - The reactant is **chemically** **adsorbed** onto the surface by **stronger** **bonds**
  - Chemisorption causes **bond** **weakening** between the atoms of the reactants
- **Desorption** of the products

  - The bonds between the products and catalyst weaken so much that the products break away from the surface
- For example, the adsorption of hydrogen molecules onto a palladium (Pd) surface

blocks.alt: Diagram showing hydrogen atoms bonding and weakening on palladium surface, illustrating the movement and interaction of atoms with labelled arrows.
blocks.caption: The reactants are adsorbed on the catalyst surface causing bond weakening and eventually desorption of the products

blocks.md:
- In the **Haber** **process** ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>) is produced from nitrogen (N<sub>2</sub>) and hydrogen (H<sub>2</sub>)
- An **iron** **catalyst** is used which speeds up the reaction by bringing the reactants close together on the metal surface
- This increases their likelihood to react with each other
- The mode of action of the iron catalyst is as follows:

  - **Diffusion **of the nitrogen and hydrogen gas to the iron surface
  - **Adsorption **of the reactant molecules onto the iron surface by forming bonds between the iron and reactant atoms
  
    - These bonds are so strong that they weaken the covalent bonds between the nitrogen atoms in N<sub>2</sub> and hydrogen atoms in H<sub>2</sub>
    - But they are weak enough to break when the catalysis has been completed
  - **The reaction **takes place between the adsorbed nitrogen and hydrogen atoms which react with each other on the iron surface to form NH<sub>3</sub>
  - **Desorption **occurs when the bonds between the NH<sub>3</sub> and iron surface are weakened and eventually broken
  - The formed NH<sub>3</sub> **diffuses **away from the iron surface

blocks.md:
- Heterogeneous catalysts are also used in the **catalytic** **removal** of oxides of nitrogen from the exhaust gases of car engines
- The catalysts speed up the conversion of:

  - Nitrogen oxides (NO<sub>y</sub>) into **harmless nitrogen gas** (N<sub>2</sub>)
  - Carbon monoxide (CO) into carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>)
- The catalytic converter has a **honeycomb **structure containing small beads coated with **platinum, palladium, **or **rhodium metals** which act as **heterogeneous catalysts**
- The mode of action of the catalysts is as follows:

  - **Adsorption **of the nitrogen oxides and CO onto the catalyst surface
  - **The weakening **of the covalent bonds within nitrogen oxides and CO
  
    - Formation of new bonds between:
    - Adjacent nitrogen atoms to form N<sub>2</sub> molecules
    - CO and oxygen atoms to form CO<sub>2</sub> molecules
  - **Desorption **of N<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub> molecules which eventually **diffuse **away from the metal surface

blocks.alt: Diagram of a catalytic converter showing exhaust gases entering, passing through a catalyst, and exiting as clean gases.
blocks.caption: The metals in catalytic converters speed up the conversion of nitrogen oxides and carbon monoxide into nitrogen  and carbon dioxide respectively

blocks.md:
- **Homogeneous catalysis** often involves **redox reactions **in which the ions involved in catalysis undergo changes in their **oxidation number**

  - As ions of transition metals can change oxidation number they are often good catalysts
- Homogeneous catalysts are used in one step and are reformed in a later step
- This is a very **slow **reaction in which the peroxydisulfate (S<sub>2,</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2- </sup>) ions **oxidise **the **iodide **to **iodine**

- Since both the S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2-</sup> and I<sup>-</sup> ions have a negative charge, it will require a lot of energy for the ions to overcome the **repulsive** **forces** and collide with each other
- Therefore, Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) ions are used as a **homogeneous catalyst**
- The catalysis involves two **redox reactions**:

  - First, Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions are **reduced** to Fe<sup>2+</sup> by  I<sup>**-**</sup>
- Then, Fe<sup>2+</sup> is **oxidised **back to Fe<sup>**3+**</sup> by S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2-</sup>

- By reacting the reactants with a positively charged Fe ion, there are no repulsive forces, and the activation energy is significantly lowered
- The order of the two reactions does not matter

  - So, Fe<sup>2+</sup> can be first oxidised to Fe<sup>3+</sup> followed by the reduction of Fe<sup>3+</sup> to Fe<sup>2+</sup>

blocks.md: - As fossil fuels contain sulfur, burning the fuels will release sulfur dioxide which oxidises in air to sulfur trioxide, and then **dilute sulfuric acid **(H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) is formed by reaction with water. The result is acidification of rain:
- Nitrogen oxides can act as **catalysts **in the formation of acid rain by catalysing the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub> to SO<sub>3</sub>
- The formed NO gets oxidised to regenerate NO<sub>2</sub>
- The regenerated NO<sub>2</sub> molecule can again oxidise another SO<sub>2</sub> molecule to SO<sub>3</sub> which will react with rainwater to form H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and so on
